title: Equations of horizontal and vertical lines

beats.say: Welcome the student in one warm sentence. Today: two special straight lines - flat ones and upright ones. We will find what their equations look like and why one of them has a gradient and the other does not. Two sentences, then straight to the grid.
Start by letting them notice, not by telling. Plot three points on the grid - (2, -1), (2, 0) and (2, 3) - and ask what they all have in common before naming anything.

ask.prompt: Look at the points (2, -1), (2, 0) and (2, 3). What do they all have in common?
ask.lookFor: The same x-coordinate, 2. A good answer also notices the y-values differ.
ask.onMiss: Ask them to read out the x-coordinate of each point, one at a time.

beats.say: Draw the line through them. Every point on it has x = 2, however high or low you go, so the line is named x = 2. A vertical line is x = a. Say what it is, and what it is not: x does not change, y can be anything.

board.text: every point on it has the same x

beats.say: Now the flat one. Across level ground the rise is zero, so the gradient is 0, and every point has the same y - here y = -3. A horizontal line is y = c.

Make the gradient feel real. Walking on flat ground has no steepness at all: gradient 0. A sheer vertical cliff is different - you go up without moving sideways at all. Put the two side by side and ask what the run is as you climb the cliff.

board.label: Climbing the cliff, the run is ___

ask.prompt: Climbing the cliff from (-3, -2) up to (-3, 2) - how far do you move sideways?
ask.lookFor: Zero. You go up but not across.
ask.onMiss: Ask for the x-coordinate at the bottom and the top, then the difference.

beats.say: A very common slip: a horizontal line runs along the x-axis, so people name it x = something. Test it with them: the line x = 3 passes through (3, 1) and (3, -1) - that is the upright line. Name a line by the coordinate that stays fixed.

board.text: name a line by the coordinate that stays the same

ask.prompt: What is the equation of the horizontal line through (0, 3)? What stays the same all along it?
ask.lookFor: y = 3, because every point on it has y = 3. A reply of x = 3 is the common slip.
ask.onMiss: Ask: on that flat line, does x change as you move along it? Does y? Then name the one that stays fixed.

beats.say: The other slip: thinking a vertical line has gradient 0. Work it out line by line with two points on x = 2, so the learner sees where every number comes from and why the answer is undefined, not 0.

lines.say: Let's take two points on the line x = 2: the point two-comma-one and the point two-comma-five.
In a point, the first number is x and the second is y. So in two-comma-one, x is 2 and y is 1.
Same for two-comma-five: x is 2, and y is 5.
Gradient is rise divided by run. Rise is how far we go UP - the change in y. Run is how far we go ACROSS - the change in x.
Rise first. y goes from 1 up to 5, so the rise is 5 minus 1, which is 4.
Run is 2 minus 2, which is 0. x never changes, so we do not move across at all.

ask.prompt: Now you try the run. x goes from 2 to 2. How far across is that?
ask.lookFor: 0 - both x values are 2, so 2 minus 2 is 0.
ask.onMiss: Point at the two x values just written - both are 2. Ask: how much do you move across going from 2 to 2?

lines.say: Now put them into the formula: rise 4, run 0. So the gradient is 4 divided by 0.
Nothing times 0 can ever make 4, so 4 divided by 0 has no answer. We say the gradient is undefined.

ask.prompt: Can we divide 4 by zero? Think: what number times 0 gives 4?
ask.lookFor: No number works - anything times 0 is 0 - so 4 ÷ 0 has no answer: the gradient is undefined, not 0.
ask.onMiss: Try a few: 1 times 0? 10 times 0? 100 times 0? They are all 0, never 4. So is there an answer?

lines.text: vertical line: gradient is undefined - not 0
lines.say: So a vertical line's gradient is undefined. Zero is the gradient of a flat line - that's the one people mix it up with.

beats.say: One more consequence, said gently: a linear function gives exactly one y for each x. A vertical line has one x with infinitely many y-values, so it is not the graph of a linear function. Do not turn this into a quiz.

board.text: x = a is not the graph of a linear function: one x, many y

beats.say: Worked example 1: find the equation and the gradient of the line through (3, -5) and (7, -5). Write the coordinates, work out the gradient, then decide whether it is horizontal or vertical and name it.
Their turn. A line passes through (-5, 8) and (-5, -3). Ask for the equation, the gradient, and which axis it is parallel to. Let them work it out; hint only when stuck.

ask.prompt: A line passes through (-5, 8) and (-5, -3). What is its equation, what is its gradient, and which axis is it parallel to?
ask.lookFor: x = -5, gradient undefined, parallel to the y-axis. All three parts, with the reasoning for the gradient.
ask.onMiss: Ask for the x-coordinates of the two points, then which kind of line that gives and what the run is.

beats.say: Close on the idea that confuses most students: why a line that runs parallel to the x-axis is named y = -3 and not x = -3.

ask.prompt: The flat line runs parallel to the x-axis. So why is it called y = -3, not x = -3?
ask.lookFor: Because every point on it has y = -3; the equation names the value that stays the same.
ask.onMiss: Ask them to list three points on the line and read off their coordinates.
